body_markdown:
Forty years ago, Vancouver, British Columbia, welcomed the world to Expo ’86—only the second time a world’s fair had been held in Canada. The event focused on[transportation](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/cars-of-worlds-fair-1964-new-york-worlds-fair/) and communication and included Highway ’86, an all-gray rolling installation crammed with all sorts of conveyances—a Honda Civic, a Datsun 240Z, a Fiat 500—along with sailboats, bicycles, a WWII submarine, and a canoe. Of course it had a canoe. This *is* Canada.


The show also featured a monorail and fully automated, driverless SkyTrain, built to showcase the “future” of people-moving. While we love any technology that has a[Simpsons show tune dedicated to it](https://youtu.be/v4z_9NcIJXI?si=DSxrxfQnChnMOZ-2&t=36) , and the SkyTrain still courses through the city, it was a vehicle hidden deep in one of the Expo ’86 exhibits that stood out. Unlike anything show-goers would have ever seen before, it, too, was a vision of the future—but one that hailed from a half-century earlier.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


It was called the *Spirit of Tomorrow* —sorry, that should read *is* called the *Spirit of Tomorrow* . That’s because, like the parts of Expo ’86 that survive today, still relevant in the midpoint of the 2020s, this car remains 100% functional. Oh, and by the way, it currently has a Mustang V-8 mounted in the middle.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


## The Shape of Water


Early automobile aerodynamics were a dark art, with most of the efforts from the 1920s and ’30s yielding the coefficient of drag of a four-by-eight sheet of plywood.[Sleek cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-death-eaters-chapter-1-tatra-t87/) like the Tatra 77 or the Chrysler Airflow tend to stand out simply because they are the exceptions to the rule.


However, in a workshop in a rural area of Vancouver Island, a restless inventor wasn’t satisfied with the status quo. His name was Horace Basil Oldfield—everyone called him Barney, after the Indy 500 racer—and he was the kind of character you might find in a Disney live-action movie. He built the area’s first bulldozer, as well as an underslung-cab logging truck that could carry six times as much timber as a modern truck could carry today.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The house in the background of the above picture—he built that too, and his granddaughter currently lives in it. It rotates 360 degrees to chase the sun, using the motor out of an old washing machine, gears, and railway-style girders, and it still functions perfectly after decades. All the electricity and plumbing run through a central umbilical cord that can’t be tangled.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


In short, Barney Oldfield was a sort of timber country Leonardo DaVinci, and he counted flight among his interests. Unlike DaVinci’s purely theoretical flying machines, however, Oldfield was an actual pilot, and starting in 1938, he began building a car that incorporated some of the elements of the aircraft of the day.


He didn’t have a wind tunnel, but there was a creek nearby. Oldfield hand-carved wooden models and dipped them into the water, watching how the eddies moved across the surface of the object, planning how he would craft an aluminum skin to do the same with air at a larger scale.


## Run Fast, Run Long


Underneath, the *[Spirit of Tomorrow](https://www.spiritoftomorrow.com/)* is some kind of Dodge sedan. No one can really remember what year it’s from, and not much of the original layout remains, anyway. For one thing, the engine Oldfield originally installed, a flathead Ford V-8, along with its current 289-cubic-inch Mustang V-8, are mounted amidships.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


You climb into the forward cockpit after getting in a door on the left-hand side, clambering over a low seat back and wedging yourself behind an angled steering wheel with a three-on-the-tree manual shifter. None of the front windows open, so while the car hails from an era where drivers still mostly used hand signals, it has electric turn signals, probably the earliest machine on the West Coast to have them.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Oldfield and his friend John Norton, along with Oldfield’s brother Brian, took several years to finish the *Spirit of Tomorrow* , and the car went through some iterations over the years. Originally, it had a large dorsal fin for stability, and the exhaust routing for the flathead V-8 exited through the roof.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


If it were merely an interesting project that rarely left the garage, this car would be a fascinating piece of engineering. As an actual car that Oldfield drove all over the length and breadth of the Pacific Northwest, it’s completely bonkers. The town of Kitimat is a thousand miles to the north, and Oldfield took his *Spirit* *of Tomorrow* at least that far at a time long before modern highways opened up the province.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Today, on those modern highways, the car would have little trouble keeping up with traffic. Actually, you’d have to watch your speed; with that ‘Stang V-8 on board, it’s really quite punchy. A slight on-center slack in the steering wheel and its modest brakes are the only old-car elements in a very stable platform that wants to run quickly despite being an octogenarian.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The Saanich Peninsula, where this car was born, is about as close to paradise as you can get on the west coast of Canada, and most of Oldfield’s family still lives in the area. The *Spirit of Tomorrow* is in the care of his niece, Arlene, who everyone calls Barnie. She’s married to Tim Lindsay, who was good friends with Uncle Barney. Oldfield’s nephew Rob runs the service station that sits up front of the old workshop. Between the three of them, the car still runs true and turns up regularly at parades and other events.


Barney Oldfield died in 1977, but almost 50 years later, his vision of the future still works faithfully. And, when any automaker trots out the latest model and brags about its low coefficient of drag, another little piece of his legacy is proved. The *Spirit of Tomorrow* was right about the future.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)
